structured_output.hypothesis: In sunflower capitula, the two families of contact spirals (parastichies) cross at a roughly constant angle across the disc, and that angle is rarely 90°.
structured_output.pass_criterion: From seed-centre coordinates of at least 20 capitula, the local crossing angle between the two parastichy families, measured at each seed, has a within-capitulum coefficient of variation of 15% or less over the radial range 0.3–0.9 R. In at least 80% of capitula, the median crossing angle also differs from 90° by more than 5°.
structured_output.fail_criterion: The within-capitulum coefficient of variation of the crossing angle exceeds 25% in more than half of capitula (angle not constant). Alternatively, the median crossing angle lies within 5° of 90° in more than 50% of capitula (orthogonality is common, not rare).
structured_output.interpretation: 'Spirals' means the contact parastichies, the visible left- and right-handed families of seeds or florets. 'Isogonal' means a constant crossing angle, as for logarithmic spirals about a common pole. 'Orthogonal' means a 90° crossing, as Church's model had it. A modern reinterpretation is needed. Real capitula follow Fermat (Vogel) spiral packing with a divergence angle near 137.5°, so the parastichies are not exact logarithmic spirals. In the Fermat model the crossing angle drifts toward 90° with distance from the centre, and near the rim it is nearly orthogonal. The test therefore asks two things. First, is the angle approximately constant over the disc? Second, is it typically non-orthogonal? The claim as stated is that orthogonality is only a rare particular case, and that is the part tested.
structured_output.no_dataset_reason: I could not identify, with confidence in its exact title, DOI or URL, a public dataset of sunflower capitulum seed or floret centre coordinates or parastichy crossing angles. Such a dataset would need per-seed positions in a single disc. Public sunflower data I know of are genomic, phenotypic or agronomic, not disc geometry. Specimen portals such as MorphoSource, iDigBio and GBIF do not reliably hold standardized capitulum images or coordinates. Under the no-fabrication rule, an honest null is the right answer here. The test could be run on new photographs of capitula with seed centres digitised.
